title: "Godzilla -1.0" and a Dream of a Post-War Recovery

commenti.body:
>If all the authority (from both sides of the Pacific) were to step back, everything would be okay. The people would solve the problem. This being a Japanese story, it does take all the people pooling their knowledge and resources to get that kaiju off their land

I really liked this movie, but this feels like a natural extension of Japan's reluctance to acknowledge all of the horrible stuff they did during the war. Yes, it's "the people" rather than the government that takes care of Godzilla, but all of these people happen to be former military. Without the interference of higher authorities, the noble Japanese army is able to save the day.

Also a quick note, the original Godzilla was released in 1954, so this is its 69th anniversary, not its 70th.

> Without the interference of higher authorities, the noble Japanese army is able to save the day.

I think Noda's little speech where he criticizes the Japanese military for how it handled the war is *trying* to be anti-war and critique the cultural decay that led Japan to where it was. But I do agree that to really resound it probably needed a little more jabs at what Japan did *to* other peoples to not value life, not just bemoan the kamikaze and banzai charges that wasted Japanese life.

> Also a quick note, the original Godzilla was released in 1954, so this is its 69th anniversary, not its 70th.

To add onto the correction here, it wasn't released *on* the 70th anniversary, but it's being released *as* Toho's 70th anniversary celebration film (just early).

i think the movie lays the blame for the war on the authorities, which would encompass the military - seeing as how the army and the navy decided on what direction the country was headed in the name of the Emperor. 

many of the people who save Tokyo are ex-military but they are there by choice and that is an important distinction. in the meeting scene, a few of them who are called there decide to leave and are not chastised for doing so at all.

 this reminds me of how the movie handles the issue of survival guilt and it has to do with the military ethos as well. "dying with honor" is the kind of bushido mumbo jumbo that the military sold the people. serve and die for the sake of the Emperor...just like the samurai did in the glorious past. when Shikishima gets eyed as someone who backed out, the mechanic Tachibana comes over and voices his support only to turn on him when Shikishima is unable to fire at Godzilla from his plane and all of Tachibana's colleagues die. i think the movie forgives Shikishima for this considering how useless it would have been to fire on Godzilla. both Shikishima and Tachibana have to work thru this guilt for them to come up with their variation on the final plan of attack.   


as for the 70th anniversary, that is how the movie is being marketed. u should email Toho.
You stated that it was released on the 70th anniversary, which it wasn’t. That’s different than being released to celebrate the anniversary, even if it’s early

this movies was made by Japanese filmmakers for a Japanese audience. i'm sure they knew it was going to have an international release but what ur asking for wasn't gonna happen with this particular movie.

As far as this movie's rather narrow criticism of wartime Japan, it should be noted that Yamazaki previously directed The Eternal Zero, a film that touches on the same ideas regarding Kamikaze pilots and was adapted from a book written by a right-wing nationalist who has repeatedly denied that Japanese war crimes ever happened.

> he criticizes the Japanese military for how it handled the war is trying to be anti-war and critique the cultural decay that led Japan to where it was. But I do agree that to really resound it probably needed a little more jabs at what Japan did to other peoples to not value life, not just bemoan the kamikaze and banzai charges that wasted Japanese life.

I haven't seen the movie yet, but plan to see it tomorrow.  But this sounds reminiscent of the  2008 movie (and [events it was based on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_July_plot)) Valkyrie.   The officers who tried to kill Hitler had criticisms of how Hitler was handling the war, but not the war itself.
